subject: Critical Thinking
title: Straw Man: Fighting an Argument Nobody Made
description: A 60-second lesson on Straw Man: Fighting an Argument Nobody Made.

hook.text: 'We should reduce military spending.' 'So you want to leave us completely defenseless?' Nobody said that.

buildup.text: Straw man: misrepresenting someone's argument to make it easier to attack, then defeating the distorted version.

discovery.text: It works by exaggeration, oversimplification, or taking a position to its most extreme possible interpretation.

twist.text: Straw men are often unintentional. We genuinely misunderstand opposing views because we don't listen carefully.

climax.text: The antidote: 'steelmanning' — restating the opponent's argument in its strongest possible form before responding.

punchline.text: If you can't state their argument fairly, you haven't understood it.

quiz.question: What is 'steelmanning'?
options: Restating the opponent's argument in its strongest form before responding

details.summary: A straw man misrepresents someone's argument into a weaker version and then attacks the distortion. The original argument is never addressed because a caricature has taken its place.
details.whyItMatters: Straw manning is everywhere in media and debate. If you cannot recognize it, you will often be persuaded that an argument has been refuted when it has not even been addressed.
takeaways: Straw manning substitutes a distorted version of the real argument
The distortion is always easier to attack than the original
The antidote is steelmanning — addressing the strongest version

faq.question: How can you tell if someone is using a straw man against your argument?
faq.answer: If their rebuttal attacks a position you did not take, they are straw-manning. Ask them to repeat your argument in their own words before responding. This forces engagement with what you actually said.

faq.question: Is accidental straw manning possible when someone genuinely misunderstands?
faq.answer: Yes. Not all straw men are deliberate. Genuine miscommunication can create unintentional distortions. Applying the principle of charity and clarifying the actual position often resolves these accidental straw man situations.
